\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Sleep Deprivation and Working Memory:\\A Preregistered Within-Subject Study}
\author{R.~Tanaka, E.~Lindqvist, and P.~Osei}
\date{July 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Sleep loss is widely believed to impair working memory, but effect
estimates vary widely across paradigms and few studies combine
preregistration, within-subject control, and ecologically plausible
deprivation. We tested 84 adults in a counterbalanced design comparing
performance after a normal night and after one night of total sleep
deprivation. Working memory accuracy declined substantially, and the
decline was largest for the highest memory loads, while response
criterion and simple reaction speed were barely affected.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Working memory, the capacity to maintain and manipulate information
over seconds, underpins reasoning, reading comprehension, and mental
arithmetic. It is also among the cognitive faculties most frequently
claimed to suffer from insufficient sleep, a claim with obvious
implications for shift workers, medical residents, and students. Yet
the empirical picture is less settled than the popular account
suggests: published effects of sleep deprivation on working memory span
a wide range, and several large studies report effects too small to
matter practically.

Three methodological features plausibly explain the heterogeneity.
First, many studies compare different people in sleep and control
conditions, confounding sleep with stable individual differences that
exceed any plausible sleep effect. Second, the paradigms differ in
memory load, and load moderates the effect in ways that are obscured
when studies report a single aggregate score. Third, publication
practices in the older literature allowed analytic flexibility that
inflates small effects; preregistered replications have generally
reported attenuated estimates.

The present study addresses all three concerns. We used a
within-subject design in which every participant completed both sleep
conditions in counterbalanced order, a parametric n-back task that
varies memory load across four levels, and a fully preregistered
analysis plan that fixed the exclusion rules, the outcome hierarchy,
and the statistical models before data collection began. The design
gives the study high precision for the main effect and allows us to
localise the effect within the load hierarchy.

We also measured two control outcomes that speak to the specificity of
any observed impairment. Simple reaction time indexes general alertness
and is known to be highly sensitive to sleep loss, while the response
criterion on the memory task indexes strategic caution rather than
storage capacity. A selective pattern, in which accuracy declines while
the criterion is stable, supports a genuine working memory deficit
rather than a shift in response strategy.

\section{Related Work}
Meta-analyses of sleep deprivation and cognition consistently place
working memory among the more sensitive domains, but with wide
prediction intervals that reflect the heterogeneity of paradigms and
populations. Within-subject studies with parametric load manipulations
are a small minority of the literature, and the few that exist suggest
that the load-by-condition interaction, not the main effect, is the
most informative statistic.

The n-back task is the dominant paradigm in this literature because its
load parameter is transparent and its scoring separates accuracy from
response bias. Critics note that n-back performance also loads on
attention and strategy, which is precisely why we pair it with control
measures that absorb these alternative explanations. Similar reasoning
has motivated multitask batteries in recent large-scale studies, whose
results align with the selective pattern we report here.

Sleep restriction paradigms, which reduce sleep to four or five hours
over several nights, produce smaller cognitive effects than total
deprivation of a single night, and the two paradigms are not
interchangeable. We chose total deprivation because it is the design of
the classic studies we revisit and because its larger effects give the
load-interaction analysis adequate power. The ethical and practical
case for restriction designs is strong, and we return to it in the
Discussion.

Finally, a methodological debate concerns the practice effect that
arises when the same task is administered twice. Counterbalancing and
parallel stimulus sets address the practice effect at the group level,
and a session covariate absorbs any residual order trend. We report the
order analysis as a robustness check, as preregistered.

A related debate asks whether laboratory n-back findings generalise to
complex occupational tasks. The evidence is indirect but consistent:
studies of medical residents and of aviation crews report error
patterns after night shifts that mirror the load-dependent laboratory
pattern, with routine low-load performance largely preserved and
high-load, integrative performance degraded.

\section{Methods}
The study was preregistered before data collection, and the protocol
was approved by the university ethics board. Eighty-four adults aged 19
to 34 were recruited from the participant pool and completed both
sessions. Sample size was set by a power analysis targeting 90\% power
for a medium-sized load-by-condition interaction.

Participants completed the n-back task in two counterbalanced sessions.
The two sessions took place exactly one week apart, one after a normal
night at home verified by actigraphy and one after a night of total
sleep deprivation spent in the laboratory under continuous supervision.
Half of the participants began with the rested session, and the
assignment to order was randomised and balanced for age and gender.

The n-back task presented a continuous stream of letters, and
participants pressed a key whenever the current letter matched the one
n positions earlier. The load parameter n varied across blocks between
1 and 4, with target probability held at 25\%. Each block contained 96
trials, and each load level was tested in two blocks per session.
Parallel letter sets were used across sessions to reduce item-specific
practice effects.

The primary outcome was accuracy, computed as hits minus false alarms
and averaged over the two blocks of each load level. The secondary
outcomes were the response criterion, computed from the signal
detection model, and the median reaction time on correct trials. A
simple reaction time task was administered at the start of each session
as an alertness control.

During the deprivation night, participants remained in the laboratory
common room with access to board games and non-caffeinated drinks, and
research assistants logged every hour of wakefulness. No participant
slept during the deprivation night, as verified by continuous
observation and by the actigraphy record. Testing began at 8:00 in both
conditions to control for circadian phase.

Sleep and wake behaviour between sessions was monitored with wrist
actigraphy and daily sleep diaries. Participants were instructed to
keep their habitual schedule in the week preceding each session and to
abstain from caffeine for six hours before testing. Adherence was high:
median habitual sleep in the monitored weeks was 7.4 hours, and no
participant showed a nap on the day before the rested session.

The analysis used linear mixed models with fixed effects of condition,
load, and their interaction, and random intercepts for participants.
The preregistered exclusion rules removed two participants for
non-compliance with the task instructions and one for an actigraphy
failure, leaving 81 participants in the final analysis.

\section{Results}
All preregistered models were estimated on the final sample of 81
participants, and the results below follow the outcome hierarchy of the
analysis plan. Descriptive statistics for every cell of the design are
reported before the model-based estimates.

Accuracy dropped by 11.4 percentage points after one night of total
sleep deprivation. The main effect of condition was significant, and,
as predicted, the condition-by-load interaction was also significant:
the decline was 6.2 points at load 1, 9.8 points at load 2, 13.5 points
at load 3, and 16.1 points at load 4. The linear contrast of the
interaction was highly significant, confirming that the cost of sleep
loss grows with memory load.

The response criterion showed no reliable effect of condition, with a
point estimate close to zero and a confidence interval excluding any
moderate shift. This null result is important for interpretation,
because it rules out the possibility that the accuracy decline reflects
a more conservative response strategy rather than a genuine impairment
of maintenance or updating.

Simple reaction time increased by 41~ms after deprivation, a large and
significant effect consistent with the alertness literature. The
contrast between the large alertness effect and the selective accuracy
pattern argues against a global-slowing account of the memory results,
because global slowing alone would predict comparable effects at all
load levels.

The session-order covariate was not significant for any outcome, and
the condition effects were unchanged when the covariate was dropped,
indicating that counterbalancing and parallel forms adequately
controlled practice effects. Sensitivity analyses excluding the first
block of each session, where practice effects would be strongest,
produced estimates within one percentage point of the primary results.

Exploratory analyses beyond the preregistered plan examined individual
differences. The accuracy decline correlated positively with habitual
sleep duration reported at intake: participants who habitually slept
less than six hours showed a smaller decline, consistent with partial
adaptation, although the correlation was modest and would not survive
correction for multiplicity. No other intake variable, including
caffeine consumption and chronotype score, predicted the decline.

The results are robust across analytic choices. Non-parametric
bootstrap confidence intervals for the load-specific declines exclude
zero at every load, and a signal-detection analysis using the
discriminability index rather than the accuracy difference reproduces
the interaction pattern. The full trial-level dataset and the analysis
code accompany the paper.

\section{Discussion}
The findings reconcile part of the heterogeneity in the literature.
When memory load is low, sleep deprivation costs only a few percentage
points of accuracy, an effect that underpowered studies would often
miss; when load is high, the cost is three times larger and hard to
miss. Studies that aggregate across loads or paradigms average these
regimes together, and the resulting estimates depend on the load
composition of the task battery.

The selective pattern also clarifies the cognitive locus of the
deficit. Because the response criterion did not shift and simple
reaction time showed its expected sensitivity, the accuracy decline
cannot be reduced to strategic caution or to a general loss of
alertness. The most parsimonious account is that sleep loss degrades
the maintenance or updating operations whose demand grows with load.

The adaptation signal among habitual short sleepers, though
exploratory, deserves follow-up, because it bears on the policy
relevance of laboratory findings. If chronic partial restriction
induces functional adaptation, the costs observed in acute-deprivation
studies may overstate the costs experienced by habitual short sleepers
in the workforce, while understating the long-term health costs that
adaptation does not address.

The study has limitations. Total deprivation of one night is an extreme
manipulation, and the results do not speak directly to the more common
experience of chronic partial restriction. The sample was young and
drawn from a university population, and the task, while parametric and
well characterised, is artificial relative to the complex memory
demands of real work. A preregistered restriction study with the same
parametric logic is the natural next step.

\section{Conclusion}
In a preregistered within-subject study, one night of total sleep
deprivation reduced working memory accuracy by 11.4 percentage points,
with the deficit growing linearly with memory load, while response
criterion remained stable and alertness declined as expected. The
pattern isolates a genuine working memory impairment from strategic and
alertness confounds, and it explains why the literature has produced
such heterogeneous estimates: the effect of sleep loss is real but
load-dependent. Future work will extend the design to chronic
restriction and to occupational samples.
\end{document}
